records.text: The user wants short folklore pieces rewritten in a chatty, lively, easy-to-understand voice inspired by Roald Dahl, with dry wording removed while preserving every detail.

In a folk tale, Gonzo was an expert river trout (iwana) fisherman who took up fishing in summer when he did not feel like blacksmithing. One day he caught enough trout to fill a bamboo basket. Returning along a mountain road, he saw a small, shaven-headed, Buddhist-monk-like ghost figure standing in grass beside a stone marker at the village entrance. As he watched, it grew into a huge norikoshi monster that seemed to reach through the clouds. Gonzo was terrified and reportedly ran all the way home.

Tetsuzo of Tsuchibuchi village told a story about strange occurrences at Taimagura Pond, opposite Oguni village on Mount Hayachine. A man from Shimomura went fishing for iwana deep in the mountains and saw a red-faced old man, identified as a tengu, and a young girl dressed strangely in the shadow of a rocky cavern. Near Taimagura, ancient, nearly circular rock dwellings stand on both sides of a stream; each is about three metres wide, with an entrance about one metre high. People reportedly lived in them in the past, and it seems someone may still be there. Tetsuzo said he could hear a nearby rooster crow if he listened carefully while fishing. The story was from about ten years before it was told.

A hairy-faced man with unusually colored eyes came from Sekiguchi Valley to Yamada Bay in Shimohei to buy goods on market days. Local people suspected he was not an ordinary human, killed him, and buried him on the bay's “larger island”; afterward, the number of fish caught in the bay declined. The island was also called Dutch Island because the Dutch ship Breskens landed there on June 10, 1643, seeking food and water. Yamada residents welcomed the crew, but on July 28 the crew was arrested and taken to Tokugawa Iemitsu in Edo, the national capital, where the Dutch were imprisoned for four months. Around that period, European ships visited the area seeking Japanese gold mines. Old man Tora of Tsuchibuchi village told the tale; as a young man, he transported packhorses to Yamada.
records.topic: Tono folk legends and local history

records.text: In winter 1913, hunter Kikuchi Eisaku of Wano in Tochinai spent a day hunting in the Oide mountains near Mount Hayachine. In the soft evening light, while trying to find a small hut, he encountered a man whose round eyes glared defensively. Kikuchi asked where he was going; the man said he was headed to a hut in the pastureland, pushed through dense brush, and hurried away. It seemed unlikely anyone would be at the pasture hut in winter, and the dim light made the man's features difficult to see. The man was about two metres tall, roughly Kikuchi's age, wore a common tight-sleeved rough-linen coat, and carried a bag-like object made from wisteria vines over his shoulder. Kikuchi was then about 25 or 26. His friend Sasaki Kizen heard the story directly from him.

Around 1920, a child from Komaki in Matsuzaki village encountered a large man on Mount Nishinai around noon in September or October, while people were gathering hagi (bush clover) to feed horses. The child peeked from behind bushes and saw the man wearing a common tight-sleeved rough-cotton coat and carrying a wisteria-vine bag with several snakes squirming inside. The frightened child crouched in the bushes as the man hurried past, then ran back to the village, relieved to be alive. The narrator heard the tale from young people one night in January during children's New Year games.

In the 1870s, the wife of a cloth dyer in Shinmachi went to visit a sick relative in Shimokumi-cho. Around 9 p.m., at the corner of Shimoyoko-cho, she saw a roughly three-metre-tall priest-like monster called a dainyudo. She fled as it chased her, flapping its coat sleeves like wings to frighten her. At the Ayabun house in Muika-machi, she was exhausted and noticed the flapping had stopped. Thinking she was safe, she turned around and saw the monster directly behind her, taller than the house's three-storey roof. She ran with all her strength to her relative's house; afterward her legs swelled and never returned to normal.

entities: Inspiration, Infallibility, and Inerrancy: Hath God Said?

records.text: In the YouTube lecture shared by the user on 2023-08-01, R.C. Sproul explains inspiration as divine superintendence through which human authors convey God’s Word. He says classical Christian theology does not specify the precise mode of inspiration, and rejects both a mechanical view that reduces authors to automatons and a dictation view in which God simply supplies the words. He distinguishes inspiration from ordinary descriptions such as an “inspired” performance.

In the YouTube lecture shared by the user on 2023-08-01, R.C. Sproul distinguishes inerrancy, meaning that Scripture does not err, from infallibility, meaning that Scripture cannot err. He argues that infallibility is the stronger claim, and that if Scripture is inspired it is infallible and therefore inerrant.
records.topic: Christian theology; biblical inerrancy and infallibility

records.text: R.C. Sproul describes the International Council on Biblical Inerrancy as an organization formed in the late 1970s to study biblical authority, inspiration, infallibility, and inerrancy. He says its first summit was held in Chicago in 1978 and produced a statement on Scripture accompanied by affirmations and denials. Sproul says he wrote a commentary on the document, “Explaining Inerrancy,” and recommends it to readers seeking to understand the debate.
records.topic: Christian theology; International Council on Biblical Inerrancy

records.text: In the YouTube lecture shared by the user on 2023-08-01, R.C. Sproul argues that inerrancy has been unfairly treated as a shibboleth associated with anti-intellectual fundamentalism. He says the term needs careful definition: inerrancy does not require grammatical perfection or absolute scientific precision, but means Scripture is consistent with its own definition of truth.
records.topic: Christian theology; debate over biblical inerrancy
